extracted.intended_audience: educated general-public readers of Popular Science Monthly; lay readers interested in science, history of mathematics, and natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for judging explanatory theories (science vs theology), and for assessing systems of numeration/notation and skeletal identification; i.e., how to judge the merits of numeral radices, positional notation, and what counts as a satisfactory explanation in science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiable evidence required for explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is not whether an explanation can be given, but whether the given explanation has any verifiable evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific method demands evidence which can prove claims (e.g., divine origin of texts or theological interpretations). Where there is no evidence to prove the texts or where interpretations are discordant with experience, those explanations fail as scientific accounts. (Text: "the criticism of scientific method asks for the evidence which can prove these texts... In both respects the answer is unequivocal. There is no evidence to prove the texts.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement with observation/experience
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation or explanation must be in agreement with fact and observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations that are discordant with experience are rejected; historical progress replaces supernatural/metempirical explanations with natural and experimental ones (Text: "the interpretations are discordant with experience..."). This is used to judge theological explanations versus scientific ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude supernatural/metempirical conceptions from scientific framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific investigation of nature and human nature should set aside supernatural and metempirical conceptions because these cannot enter into the framework of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be scientific, moral and physical facts should be investigated and systematized on the same principles — i.e., natural and experimental methods — excluding supernatural explanations (Text: "setting aside in the one as in the other all supernatural and metempirical conceptions, because these cannot enter into the framework of knowledge").

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of local values (positional notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each symbol has an intrinsic and a local value; positional (Hindoo) notation's chief excellence arises from this principle of 'local values'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positional notation requires only a small set of significant digits plus a zero; local value (position) multiplies a digit by powers of the radix, enabling ease of expressing numbers and great simplicity in computations and decimal fractions (Text: "Its chief excellence, however, arises from its principle of 'local values.' ... Another peculiar merit appears when fractions are involved, in the facility with which 'decimal' fractions may be used.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: A superior notation uses relatively few distinct symbols to represent numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hindoo (decimal positional) notation needs only nine symbols plus zero; smaller radices increase the number of figures required to represent numbers, while larger radices reduce the number of symbols but may increase computational difficulty (Text: "It requires only nine symbols, together with the dot or zero.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease/simplicity of computation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good numeral system should make arithmetic computations simpler or less error-prone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different radices trade off manual writing and mental labor: binary minimizes mental multiplication but requires many more digits (more manual labor); tonal (16) reduces fraction length but needs extensive multiplication tables; octonary (8) is argued to be easier and to reduce mental work and errors (Text: claims about binary: "thought in arithmetical work is almost superseded"; about tonal: "The disadvantages ... are many. It requires a multiplication-table for all numbers from one to sixteen.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Radix divisibility and factorability
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable radix is divisible by many small integers (enabling bisections and common fractional subdivisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radices like 12 (duodecimal) and 8 (octonary) are praised because they admit many divisors (2, 3, 4, 6) or indefinite bisection, which simplifies common fractional work; ten is criticized because it permits only one bisection (half = 5 is odd) and is ill-suited to shop/market operations (Text: "Ten is, theoretically, ill suited... because it permits of only one bisection..." and "The duodenary or twelve scale has many striking advantages...").

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with practical/trade needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Notation should align with the practical fractional divisions used in trade (halves, quarters, eighths, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market practice often uses successive halvings (halves, quarters, eighths) rather than fifths or tenths; hence a radix that supports successive bisections better serves practical commerce (Text: "The shopman reckons by halves, quarters, eighths... and not by fifths or tenths.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness (compactness of representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: How many symbols are required to express a given number — more compact systems require fewer places/digits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binary requires many more digits (e.g., year 1878 would need 11 binary digits), tonal or larger radices express numbers more compactly; this affects manual labor and writing time (Text: "the binary scale would call for about three and a half times as many figures as the denary...").

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of common fraction representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good radix yields short/simple representations for common vulgar fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tonal (16) reduces the decimal places for common fractions (table shown); octonary and duodecimal also give simpler fractions compared to decimal for many everyday fractions (Text: table comparing denary and tonal fractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Size of arithmetic tables and mental load
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the size of multiplication/addition tables required and the consequent mental learning burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger radices (e.g., tonal/16) require more extensive multiplication tables increasing mental labor; smaller radices reduce tables but increase number length — a tradeoff to consider (Text: "It requires a multiplication-table for all numbers from one to sixteen. The mental labor of calculating would, therefore, be increased.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of computational error
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer systems that lessen the danger of error in computations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Octonary is claimed to reduce chance of error and to require less mental work than decimal; binary reduces mental arithmetic but increases manual steps which may affect error in other ways (Text: "The danger of error in computations is correspondingly lessened.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off between manual vs mental labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess systems for whether they shift burden toward manual writing or toward mental calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Binary reduces mental arithmetic (only 1 digit added) but increases number of figures (more writing); tonal reduces number of places for fractions but increases required tables and mental memory. Choose based on which labor type is more costly in context (Text: discussion of binary: "thought in arithmetical work is almost superseded... would require more figures...").

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with existing infrastructure and historical inertia
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical adoption must consider the immense existing store of arithmetical tables and formulas; theoretical superiority alone won't ensure replacement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even theoretically superior systems are unlikely to supplant decimal because of entrenched practice and the enormous body of existing computation infrastructure (Text: "the projects of those who expect to subvert it... are of course chimerical").

rubrics_metrics.name: State of preservation matters for bone identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The ability to correctly determine the identity of bones depends greatly on their state of preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly preserved bones make determination difficult; identification accuracy varies with preservation and which bone is preserved (Text: "A great deal depends on the state of preservation of the bone; and, again, what particular bone it is.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain bones are more diagnostically decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: Some single bones (e.g., teeth, bones of feet or hands) are much more decisive for identification than ribs or vertebrae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teeth and certain limb bones convey clearer taxonomic information, whereas ribs and vertebrae may be less diagnostic (Text: "Certain single bones, as the tooth, or one of the bones of the feet or hands, are much more decisive in their character than the ribs or vertebrae.").

rubrics_metrics.name: Tooth structure indicates diet and taxonomic affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of teeth relates to the character and consistency of food and thus helps determine taxonomic and ecological traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tooth morphology reflects dietary habits, providing strong evidence for classification (Text: "The structure of the teeth shows a relation to the character and consistency of the food...").

rubrics_metrics.name: Limb articulation and socket play indicate locomotion medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Bones of the limbs have greater play in their sockets in land animals vs air or water animals because flexibility is necessary for terrestrial locomotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree of mobility in limb joints informs judgments about an animal's mode of life and aids classification (Text: "In land-animals the bones of the limbs have more play in their sockets than in air or water animals, because flexibility is necessary...").
